Let's turn the photoelectric equation into a graph we can actually read.
The fastest emitted electrons have kinetic energy h times frequency minus the
work function.
A retarding potential stops even those electrons when e times the stopping
potential magnitude equals that maximum energy.
So stopping potential versus frequency is a straight line above threshold.
Its slope is h divided by e.
Its horizontal intercept is the threshold frequency, and its extrapolated
vertical intercept is minus the work function divided by e.
That vertical intercept is a mathematical extrapolation, not an emitted
electron measurement below threshold.
Take an illustrative surface with work function two electron volts.
Use h over e approximately four point one three six times ten to the minus
fifteen volt seconds.
At frequency six times ten to the fourteen hertz, stopping potential is zero
point four eight one six volts.
At ten times ten to the fourteen hertz, it is two point one three six volts.
Subtract the two stopping potentials and divide by the frequency difference.
You recover the same slope.
The threshold is approximately four point eight three six times ten to the
fourteen hertz.
Now make the light brighter without changing frequency.
Think before changing the graph.
In the ideal one photon picture, you increase photon arrival rate and can
increase photocurrent, but you do not increase the maximum energy per emitted
electron.
Saturation current and stopping potential answer different questions.
Real surfaces, contact potentials and experimental offsets require care, but
our numerical graph uses the stated ideal model.
For JEE, label the axes and their units before reading a slope.
A slope of energy against frequency gives h; a slope of voltage against
frequency gives h over e.

After paying the work function, the maximum emitted kinetic energy is one

one electron volts, and the ideal stopping potential is one point one volts.
An eight hundred nanometre photon has only one point five five electron volts.
In this ordinary one photon model, it cannot eject an electron from this

We are not discussing intense field multiphoton processes.
Next, give the four hundred nanometre beam optical power two milliwatts.
Power is energy delivered per second, so divide by photon energy in joules to

Using one electron volt approximately one point six zero two times ten to the

electrons in our stated efficiency model.
Multiply by zero point zero zero one, then by the elementary charge.
The current is about zero point six four five microamperes.
Pause and separate the two answers: one point one volts describes the maximum
electron energy, while the microampere result depends on photon rate and

Do not quietly assume every photon creates an electron that reaches the

A JEE numerical should state or justify that efficiency assumption.
Doubling optical power at fixed wavelength doubles the predicted current in
this simple linear model, but leaves the maximum kinetic energy unchanged.
For matter waves, start with momentum.
De Broglie wavelength is h divided by momentum.
It is not h divided by speed.
Two particles with the same momentum have the same wavelength even if their
masses differ.
For nonrelativistic kinetic energy K, momentum magnitude is the square root of
two m K.
Therefore wavelength is inversely proportional to the square root of mass at
equal kinetic energy.
Compare an electron and a proton with the same small kinetic energy.
Using proton mass about eighteen hundred thirty six electron masses, the
electron wavelength is about the square root of eighteen hundred thirty six
times the proton wavelength.
That ratio is approximately forty two point eight five.
Now accelerate an electron from rest through one hundred fifty volts.
Its kinetic energy is one hundred fifty electron volts.
A convenient nonrelativistic electron relation gives wavelength in angstroms
as
approximately twelve point two seven divided by the square root of the

The result is about one point zero zero two angstroms, or zero point one zero

One angstrom is ten to the minus ten metres.
What if you increase that voltage by a factor of four?
Pause.
Momentum doubles and wavelength halves, in the nonrelativistic regime.
Equal accelerating voltage is not always equal energy for different charge
magnitudes: an ion carrying twice the elementary charge gains twice the
energy.
At sufficiently large kinetic energies, the simple square root relation fails
and relativistic momentum is needed.
The core de Broglie relation still uses the correct momentum.
Our examples deliberately stay at low energy.
Distinguish equal speed, equal kinetic energy, equal accelerating voltage and
equal momentum: those phrases select different comparisons.
